What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Explain opposing financial movements using the same period, comparison, and calculation basis.
  • Clarify the reporting question and separate service timing, recognition, posting, and cash payment.
  • Present a reconciled forecast update and distinguish quantified drivers from unresolved residuals.
  • Explain conditional liquidity, test a delayed-receipt case, and distinguish available funds from unverified facilities.
  • Present a qualified performance comparison and correct misleading return language.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. These are teaching suggestions, not a certified level assessment.

01Finance Communication: Drivers, Assumptions, Materiality, RiskRevenue is ahead, but profit is behind+

Your goal

Explain opposing financial movements using the same period, comparison, and calculation basis.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

Revenue is ahead, but profit is behind

For the month, budgeted revenue was $1,000,000 and operating costs were $800,000. Actual revenue was $1,050,000 and operating costs were $854,000. The cost increase comprises $30,000 in freight and $24,000 in agency labor. The analyst has verified those categories but has not separated rate and volume effects or assessed recurrence. Lena, the analyst, and Amir, the finance director, are preparing a concise management-review explanation. All figures use the same currency and reporting scope.

Lena: Finance analyst / Amir: Finance director

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is actual operating profit in this case?

Answer and explanation

C. $196,000

Actual revenue of $1,050,000 less operating costs of $854,000 gives operating profit of $196,000.

2. How much did costs exceed budget?

Answer and explanation

B. $54,000

Subtract budgeted costs of $800,000 from actual costs of $854,000; the category increases also total $54,000.

3. Which question remains unresolved?

Answer and explanation

A. How much of the cost increase reflects rate versus volume

The briefing verifies category amounts but explicitly leaves rate, volume, and recurrence analysis incomplete.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Revenue is 5% above budget: $50,000 divided by $1,000,000. Operating profit is 2% below budget: a $4,000 decline from $200,000 to $196,000. The percentages use different denominators and must not be subtracted to explain profit.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
revenue
Income recognized from the business's goods or services under the relevant basis.report recognized revenue
operating cost
A cost included in the stated measure of operating activity.analyze operating costs
operating profit
Revenue less the operating costs included in the stated presentation.explain operating profit
gross profit
Revenue less the specified cost of goods or services sold.distinguish gross from operating profit
net income
Profit after the expenses and other items in the applicable presentation.reconcile net income
variance
A difference between a result and its stated comparator.explain a budget variance
driver
A factor contributing to a financial movement.isolate the main driver
offset
A movement that counteracts another movement.quantify the cost offset
favorable
Beneficial against the specified comparison or objective.label a favorable variance
unfavorable
Adverse against the specified comparison or objective.explain an unfavorable variance
price effect
The portion of a movement attributed to selling-price changes.separate the price effect
volume effect
The portion attributed to a change in quantities.estimate the volume effect
mix effect
The impact of a change in the composition of sales or activity.analyze the product-mix effect
rate effect
The portion attributed to a change in a cost or other unit rate.separate rate from volume
recurring
Expected to arise repeatedly under the relevant conditions.identify recurring costs
one-off
An item described as unusual or nonrecurring, subject to support.challenge a one-off classification
run rate
A projected pace based on selected current activity.qualify the implied run rate
materiality
Significance assessed in context, not solely by an arbitrary percentage.assess quantitative and qualitative materiality
assumption
An input or premise used without treating it as an established outcome.state the underlying assumption
operating margin
Operating profit divided by revenue on the specified basis.explain operating-margin movement
percentage point
One unit of difference between percentage values.report a percentage-point change
basis point
One hundredth of a percentage point.express a movement in basis points
like-for-like
Compared on a sufficiently consistent scope and basis.establish a like-for-like comparison
management commentary
Explanation accompanying reported financial information.sharpen management commentary

Freight and agency labor explain where the $54,000 cost increase sits. They do not, by themselves, establish whether higher rates, greater activity, or a temporary issue caused it. A category bridge and a causal explanation are related but different.

C Notice the language

Answer the apparent contradiction

A manager may interrupt with "How can sales be up and profit down?" Treat this as a request to connect the figures, not necessarily a personal challenge. Give the comparison and the offsetting movement first, then separate established categories from causes still being tested.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Lead with the contrast
Revenue is above budget, but operating profit is below it.
Name the offset
The $54,000 cost increase more than offsets the $50,000 revenue increase.
State the basis
These figures cover the same month, currency, and reporting scope.
Quantify the result
Operating profit is $196,000, which is $4,000 below budget.
Locate the movement
Freight and agency labor account for the identified cost increase.
Preserve uncertainty
The rate-versus-volume split remains under review.
Avoid extrapolation
We have not established that either increase is recurring.
Close with a check
I will validate the drivers before changing the forward estimate.
Clarify a comparison
Are you asking about budget, last year, or the previous forecast?
Correct a unit
That is a percentage-point change, not a percentage change.
Explain a denominator
The 2% decline is measured against budgeted operating profit.
Challenge a label
What supports calling that item one-off?
Limit causation
The category totals locate the increase but do not yet explain its cause.
Separate margins
A higher revenue total does not guarantee a higher operating margin.
Keep a caveat useful
The open question is recurrence, not whether the recorded increase exists.
Offer a concise account
Sales gained $50,000; operating costs rose by $54,000 against budget.
6 language and precision notes
Above and below
Attach the comparator: above budget is incomplete if the audience might assume above last year.
More than offset
This phrase means the opposing movement is larger, explaining why the final result changes direction.
Percent versus points
A move from 10% to 12% is two percentage points, or a 20% relative increase.
Account for
The phrase can identify a numerical contribution without establishing an underlying operational cause.
Recurrence language
"May recur" is not the same as "is recurring"; the forecast needs a supported assumption.
On the same basis
Use this only after checking period, currency, scope, and relevant measurement definitions.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which sentence correctly explains the profit movement?

Answer and explanation

A. Costs rose $54,000, exceeding the $50,000 revenue gain by $4,000.

The dollar bridge reconciles the $4,000 profit shortfall without mixing percentages with different bases.

2. Which expression accurately describes the revenue comparison?

Answer and explanation

C. Five percent above the month's budget

The $50,000 increase is 5% of the $1,000,000 monthly budget, not a different period or unit.

3. Which statement preserves the unresolved cause?

Answer and explanation

A. The categories are verified; rate and volume effects are not yet separated.

Only the categories are established; attributing specific causes would go beyond the stated review.

4. Which question most directly tests the one-off label?

Answer and explanation

C. Which costs relate to the disruption, and will those conditions continue next month?

Nonrecurrence depends on the cause and its expected persistence. Ownership, payment and the already verified category total do not settle whether the cost will recur.

E Conversations

Revenue is ahead, but profit is behind

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Lena: Finance analyst / Amir: Finance director

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • Operating margin
  • comparator
  • drivers
  • run rate
  • Materiality
  • variance
  • offset
  • volume effect
  • basis
  • one-off
  1. Amir
    The opening slide says revenue is five percent ahead, yet operating profit is two percent behind. Give me the connection before we list every account in the ledger.
  2. Lena
    The 1 is operating cost. Revenue gained fifty thousand dollars against budget, while costs rose fifty-four thousand, leaving profit four thousand below plan.
  3. Amir
    Good. Make sure ahead means ahead of this month's budget. Someone reading the slide quickly could assume the five percent is a year-on-year growth figure.
  4. Lena
    I will name the 2 in the headline. Actual profit is one hundred ninety-six thousand dollars against two hundred thousand budgeted, using the same reporting scope.
  5. Amir
    Which accounts explain the extra fifty-four thousand? Start with what you've verified, then tell me which causes still need checking.
  6. Lena
    Freight contributes thirty thousand and agency labor twenty-four thousand. Those categories explain the 3, but I have not yet separated rate and volume effects.
  7. Amir
    That distinction matters. More sales could require more activity, and a higher unit rate could also contribute. We should not call the entire increase inflation.
  8. Lena
    Agreed. The 4 needs the underlying quantity records. I will compare those with the rates rather than infer the cause from the account name.
  9. Amir
    A colleague wants both increases labeled one-off because a supplier problem occurred this month. Does that event establish that the full amounts will disappear next month?
  10. Lena
    No. The 5 description needs support. We must identify which costs relate to the event and whether the conditions causing them will continue.
  11. Amir
    Then don't call it temporary yet. What carries into next month's forecast, and what are you still asking Operations to confirm?
  12. Lena
    I will not roll the full amount into a new 6 or remove it automatically. The current actuals are known; the expected future pattern remains an analytical question.
  13. Amir
    What about operating margin? Revenue growth alone sounds encouraging, but the profit result suggests we should avoid describing the overall performance as uniformly favorable.
  14. Lena
    Yes. 7 uses profit divided by revenue. We should distinguish that ratio from the two percent decline in the profit amount against budget.
  15. Amir
    In a short update, would you say the problem is immaterial because the profit shortfall is only two percent? I do not want a casual label to close the discussion.
  16. Lena
    No. 8 requires context, including any decision or reporting implications. The small percentage alone does not establish that the matter can be ignored.
  17. Amir
    Give me the final two sentences, with the open question intact. The meeting needs the result and the next analytical step, not every intermediate calculation.
  18. Lena
    Revenue is five percent above budget, but higher costs more than offset the gain. We are validating the 9 and recurrence of the freight and agency-labor increases before revising expectations.
  19. Amir
    That works. Keep the dollar bridge available for follow-up, and ensure the period and currency remain visible when the slide is copied into the executive pack.
  20. Lena
    I will preserve the 10 and retain the unresolved checks in the commentary. The shortened version will not turn a verified category movement into a verified cause.

Answers and explanations
  1. offset Turn 2. An offset counteracts another movement; here the cost increase exceeds the revenue gain and reduces profit.
  2. comparator Turn 4. The comparator is the reference used for the measurement, here the same month's budget rather than last year.
  3. variance Turn 6. Variance is the difference from the stated reference; the two verified category amounts reconcile the total cost increase.
  4. volume effect Turn 8. The volume effect relates to changed quantities or activity; it must be separated from unit-rate changes before attributing the increase.
  5. one-off Turn 10. One-off claims nonrecurrence; one unusual event does not establish that all costs in the categories will disappear.
  6. run rate Turn 12. A run rate projects a pace from selected activity; untested recurrence makes automatic extrapolation unreliable.
  7. Operating margin Turn 14. Operating margin relates operating profit to revenue; it can decline even when the revenue amount increases.
  8. Materiality Turn 16. Materiality depends on context and qualitative factors as well as size; a single percentage does not settle significance.
  9. drivers Turn 18. Drivers explain the contributing factors; rate, volume, and recurrence checks turn category totals into a more useful causal account.
  10. basis Turn 20. The basis identifies the period, currency, scope, and definitions that make the figures comparable and interpretable.

Dialogue in the book, page 10 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Revenue ahead, operating profit behind

The lesson's review shows revenue 5% above budget and operating profit 2% below. The causes are not supplied.

  1. Finance manager: Revenue is five percent above budget, while operating profit is two percent below budget.
  2. Operations director: That sounds contradictory. Doesn't higher revenue mean the business made more operating profit?
  3. Finance manager: Revenue measures sales; operating income also reflects operating costs. The two variances can differ.
  4. Operations director: Can we say higher staff costs caused the profit shortfall in this case?
  5. Finance manager: Not from the figures provided. We haven't established the cost or mix drivers.
  6. Operations director: Then give me a one-sentence explanation that preserves what we actually know.
  7. Finance manager: Sales exceeded budget, but operating profit fell short; the reasons for that difference still need review.
  8. Operations director: That distinguishes the result from the explanation without hiding the unfavorable variance.
  9. Finance manager: Exactly. A sensitivity analysis could explore assumptions, but it wouldn't establish the actual cause.
  10. Operations director: I'll use that qualified summary and ask for the driver analysis separately.
Higher revenue per unit, unchanged unit sales

Separate fictional planning exercise: revenue rises from $100,000 to $110,000 while unit sales remain at 1,000; the revenue breakdown is available only at this level.

  1. Sales director: Revenue rose from one hundred thousand to one hundred ten thousand dollars. We sold more units, then?
  2. Finance analyst: Unit sales stayed at one thousand. Revenue growth and volume growth aren't the same here.
  3. Sales director: So the average revenue per unit moved from one hundred to one hundred ten dollars?
  4. Finance analyst: Yes, using these totals. That doesn't tell us whether pricing, discounts, or product mix changed.
  5. Sales director: I was about to credit a higher list price for the entire variance.
  6. Finance analyst: We need the detailed breakdown before making that attribution. The average alone doesn't isolate it.
  7. Sales director: Could you explain the distinction in the meeting using those two averages?
  8. Finance analyst: Certainly. The company earned more revenue per unit in aggregate, but the underlying drivers remain unconfirmed.
  9. Sales director: I'll separate the arithmetic from the pricing explanation in my remarks.
  10. Finance analyst: Good. We'll review the transaction detail before concluding which driver caused the movement.
Sensitivity is a what-if, not a forecast update

Separate fictional model review: an analyst tests a 10% fuel-cost increase without changing the approved forecast assumptions.

  1. Business manager: Your model shows fuel cost up ten percent. Has that become our new forecast?
  2. FP&A analyst: No. It's a sensitivity test showing what changes if that assumption is varied.
  3. Business manager: Then the operating-income result is conditional, not a prediction that fuel will rise that much?
  4. FP&A analyst: Correct. The approved forecast assumptions haven't been changed by this separate test.
  5. Business manager: Why show a case we don't claim will actually occur next period?
  6. FP&A analyst: It helps explain exposure: how dependent the result is on one uncertain input.
  7. Business manager: Could other costs change at the same time in a real situation?
  8. FP&A analyst: They could. This test isolates one input and doesn't describe every possible interaction.
  9. Business manager: I'll call it a fuel-cost sensitivity and keep it separate from the forecast.
  10. FP&A analyst: That preserves the distinction between exploring risk and updating our expected financial result.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Revenue is ahead, but profit is behind
  1. Read Amir and Lena's corrected exchange. Give the $50,000 revenue gain, $54,000 cost increase and $4,000 profit shortfall without subtracting the two percentages.
  2. Switch roles. Stress the unresolved rate, volume and recurrence checks; do not relabel the whole increase as inflation or one-off.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

Margin up, revenue flat

Revenue is unchanged at $500,000. Operating profit rises from $50,000 to $60,000 because costs fall by $10,000. Both periods use the same scope and accounting basis.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Analyst: "The dollar gain comes from lower ___, not higher sales."

Answer and explanation

B. costs

Unchanged revenue and a $10,000 cost reduction explain the $10,000 increase in operating profit.

2. Director: "The margin rises from 10% to 12%, a two-percentage-point ___."

Answer and explanation

A. increase

The difference between the two margin percentages is two percentage points, not a two percent relative change.

3. Analyst: "I will keep the revenue ___ unchanged in the comparison."

Answer and explanation

B. denominator

Each margin divides profit by the same $500,000 revenue, making the ratio comparison consistent.

4. Director: "Confirm whether the savings recur before changing the ___."

Answer and explanation

A. forecast

A historical cost reduction does not automatically establish the future pattern used in a forecast.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 01: Finance Communication: Drivers, Assumptions, Materiality, Risk
Original fictional case: For the month, budgeted revenue was $1,000,000 and operating costs were $800,000. Actual revenue was $1,050,000 and operating costs were $854,000. The cost increase comprises $30,000 in freight and $24,000 in agency labor. The analyst has verified those categories but has not separated rate and volume effects or assessed recurrence. Language workshop: Revenue is ahead, but profit is behind

Language guidance: Revenue is 5% above budget: $50,000 divided by $1,000,000. Operating profit is 2% below budget: a $4,000 decline from $200,000 to $196,000. The percentages use different denominators and must not be subtracted to explain profit.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Revenue is above budget, but operating profit is below it. / The $54,000 cost increase more than offsets the $50,000 revenue increase. / These figures cover the same month, currency, and reporting scope. / Operating profit is $196,000, which is $4,000 below budget. / Freight and agency labor account for the identified cost increase. / The rate-versus-volume split remains under review. / We have not established that either increase is recurring. / I will validate the drivers before changing the forward estimate. / Are you asking about budget, last year, or the previous forecast? / That is a percentage-point change, not a percentage change. / The 2% decline is measured against budgeted operating profit. / What supports calling that item one-off? / The category totals locate the increase but do not yet explain its cause. / A higher revenue total does not guarantee a higher operating margin. / The open question is recurrence, not whether the recorded increase exists. / Sales gained $50,000; operating costs rose by $54,000 against budget.

TASK: Choose grammar that preserves the meaning
1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.
3. Explain why each choice fits or fails, then ask me to read the completed exchange aloud. Do not request a draft, original written sentence or essay.

Course: Finance English
Professional audience: accounting, FP&A, treasury, banking, investments, audit, risk, corporate finance, and finance-adjacent teams
Scope: Fictional English-language practice, not investment, lending, accounting, tax, or legal advice. Definitions are concise teaching descriptions. Actual treatments and decisions require current standards, governing documents, firm policies, and qualified review. No product or transaction is recommended.
Lesson 01: Finance Communication: Drivers, Assumptions, Materiality, Risk
Original fictional case: For the month, budgeted revenue was $1,000,000 and operating costs were $800,000. Actual revenue was $1,050,000 and operating costs were $854,000. The cost increase comprises $30,000 in freight and $24,000 in agency labor. The analyst has verified those categories but has not separated rate and volume effects or assessed recurrence. Lena, the analyst, and Amir, the finance director, are preparing a concise management-review explanation. All figures use the same currency and reporting scope.
Language workshop: Revenue is ahead, but profit is behind
Communication goal: Explain opposing financial movements using the same period, comparison, and calculation basis.
Language guidance: Revenue is 5% above budget: $50,000 divided by $1,000,000. Operating profit is 2% below budget: a $4,000 decline from $200,000 to $196,000. The percentages use different denominators and must not be subtracted to explain profit.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Revenue is above budget, but operating profit is below it. / The $54,000 cost increase more than offsets the $50,000 revenue increase. / These figures cover the same month, currency, and reporting scope. / Operating profit is $196,000, which is $4,000 below budget. / Freight and agency labor account for the identified cost increase. / The rate-versus-volume split remains under review. / We have not established that either increase is recurring. / I will validate the drivers before changing the forward estimate. / Are you asking about budget, last year, or the previous forecast? / That is a percentage-point change, not a percentage change. / The 2% decline is measured against budgeted operating profit. / What supports calling that item one-off? / The category totals locate the increase but do not yet explain its cause. / A higher revenue total does not guarantee a higher operating margin. / The open question is recurrence, not whether the recorded increase exists. / Sales gained $50,000; operating costs rose by $54,000 against budget.
Vocabulary: revenue: Income recognized from the business's goods or services under the relevant basis. / operating cost: A cost included in the stated measure of operating activity. / operating profit: Revenue less the operating costs included in the stated presentation. / gross profit: Revenue less the specified cost of goods or services sold. / net income: Profit after the expenses and other items in the applicable presentation. / variance: A difference between a result and its stated comparator. / driver: A factor contributing to a financial movement. / offset: A movement that counteracts another movement. / favorable: Beneficial against the specified comparison or objective. / unfavorable: Adverse against the specified comparison or objective. / price effect: The portion of a movement attributed to selling-price changes. / volume effect: The portion attributed to a change in quantities. / mix effect: The impact of a change in the composition of sales or activity. / rate effect: The portion attributed to a change in a cost or other unit rate. / recurring: Expected to arise repeatedly under the relevant conditions. / one-off: An item described as unusual or nonrecurring, subject to support. / run rate: A projected pace based on selected current activity. / materiality: Significance assessed in context, not solely by an arbitrary percentage. / assumption: An input or premise used without treating it as an established outcome. / operating margin: Operating profit divided by revenue on the specified basis. / percentage point: One unit of difference between percentage values. / basis point: One hundredth of a percentage point. / like-for-like: Compared on a sufficiently consistent scope and basis. / management commentary: Explanation accompanying reported financial information.
Speaking task: Read Amir and Lena's corrected exchange. Give the $50,000 revenue gain, $54,000 cost increase and $4,000 profit shortfall without subtracting the two percentages. Switch roles. Stress the unresolved rate, volume and recurrence checks; do not relabel the whole increase as inflation or one-off. Read the corrected transfer twice. Keep the 10%-to-12% margin change as two percentage points, with revenue unchanged.
Partner: Lena: Finance analyst / Amir: Finance director
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: Revenue is unchanged at $500,000. Operating profit rises from $50,000 to $60,000 because costs fall by $10,000. Both periods use the same scope and accounting basis.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Amir: Give me the final two sentences, with the open question intact. The meeting needs the result and the next analytical step, not every intermediate calculation.
Lena: Revenue is five percent above budget, but higher costs more than offset the gain. We are validating the drivers and recurrence of the freight and agency-labor increases before revising expectations.
Amir: That works. Keep the dollar bridge available for follow-up, and ensure the period and currency remain visible when the slide is copied into the executive pack.
Lena: I will preserve the basis and retain the unresolved checks in the commentary. The shortened version will not turn a verified category movement into a verified cause.
END REFERENCE

02Financial Statements, Close, and Accounting JudgmentsDecember service, January invoice, January payment+

Your goal

Clarify the reporting question and separate service timing, recognition, posting, and cash payment.

This lesson in the book, page 13 ↗

A Read the situation

December service, January invoice, January payment

A supplier performed a December maintenance service. The $12,000 invoice was dated 5 January and paid on 20 January. The approved policy for this fictional case expenses this type of service when received. Before confirming the December entry, accounting must verify completion and check whether an accrual was already posted. Sofia, an accountant, and Chen, the controller, are reviewing the close schedule. No new journal entry has been approved.

Sofia: Accountant / Chen: Controller

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. In which month did the cash payment occur?

Answer and explanation

A. January

The invoice was paid on 20 January; that cash date is distinct from service delivery and expense recognition.

2. What checks are required before the December entry is confirmed?

Answer and explanation

D. Service completion and whether an accrual already exists

Completion evidence supports the stated expense policy; checking prior accruals prevents duplication. Payment, identity and matching amounts do not establish both points.

3. What entry has been approved?

Answer and explanation

C. No new journal entry

The briefing explicitly leaves the new entry unapproved pending the specified accounting checks.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Under the expressly stated case policy, December service receipt is relevant to the expense period. January payment belongs to January cash reporting. The invoice date alone does not answer both questions, and an existing accrual must be checked before another expense is posted.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
income statement
A report of income and expenses over a stated period.review the income statement
balance sheet
A statement of assets, liabilities, and equity at a stated date.reconcile a balance-sheet account
cash flow statement
A report of cash movements classified under the relevant framework.explain the cash flow statement
reporting period
The interval covered by a financial report.identify the reporting period
period-end close
Procedures used to finalize records for a reporting period.complete the period-end close
cutoff
Assignment of transactions to the appropriate accounting period.test transaction cutoff
recognition
Recording an item in financial statements when relevant criteria are met.assess expense recognition
accrual
Recognition of income or expense before related cash is received or paid.review the expense accrual
accrued liability
A recorded obligation for an incurred cost not yet settled.substantiate an accrued liability
accounts payable
Amounts owed to suppliers for goods or services received.reconcile accounts payable
prepayment
Payment recorded before the related expense is recognized.release a prepayment to expense
deferred revenue
Amount recorded as a liability before related revenue is recognized.analyze deferred revenue
journal entry
A recorded set of debits and credits.approve a journal entry
general ledger
The central record of financial accounts and postings.inspect the general ledger
subledger
Detailed records supporting a general-ledger account.reconcile the subledger
posting date
The date used to record an entry in a system.verify the posting date
reversing entry
An entry that offsets an earlier entry under the relevant process.check the reversing entry
true-up
An adjustment aligning an estimate with updated support.calculate the required true-up
supporting schedule
A detailed record explaining a reported balance.maintain the supporting schedule
account reconciliation
Comparison and explanation of records supporting an account balance.complete the account reconciliation
accounting estimate
An amount measured using judgment and available information.document an accounting estimate
accounting policy
The principles and methods used for a class of transactions.apply the approved accounting policy
capitalization
Recording qualifying expenditure as an asset rather than an immediate expense.assess capitalization criteria
audit trail
Records that allow a transaction and its approvals to be traced.preserve the audit trail

A journal can balance mathematically and still be wrong in period, account, amount, or support. Approval of an entry and confirmation of service completion are different controls. Follow the applicable framework and policy for actual transactions, not this fictional example alone.

C Notice the language

Clarify which date answers the question

A colleague asking "Which month?" may mean the expense period, invoice date, payment month, or posting period. Name the purpose of the schedule before choosing a date. Precision about accounting judgments is more useful than confident repetition of a familiar rule.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Clarify the schedule
Are we showing expense recognition or the cash payment date?
State the sequence
Service was in December; invoicing and payment occurred in January.
Apply the case policy
The stated policy expenses this service when received.
Request support
Please provide evidence that the December service was completed.
Check duplication
Was a December accrual already recorded for this supplier?
Limit approval
The new entry is not approved until the supporting checks are complete.
Separate records
The invoice date and reporting period need not answer the same question.
Close the review
I will reconcile the existing balance before proposing an adjustment.
Trace the amount
Which schedule supports the $12,000 balance?
Check a reversal
Has the earlier accrual reversed, and in which posting period?
Name the adjustment
Is this a new expense or a true-up of an existing estimate?
Preserve evidence
Link the service confirmation and invoice to the journal support.
Avoid a shortcut
Payment timing alone does not determine expense recognition here.
Specify the account
Which ledger account contains the original accrual?
Keep status clear
Prepared for review is not the same as approved for posting.
Confirm the handoff
The remaining checks are completion evidence and the existing accrual.
6 language and precision notes
Occurred versus posted
A service occurs on operational dates; an entry is posted to accounting records. Do not merge those events.
Already and yet
"Already accrued" tests duplication, while "not yet approved" states the current authorization limit.
Which month for what
Pair every date with its purpose: service month, invoice date, cash date, or reporting period.
Under the policy
This phrase ties the treatment to the stated case rule instead of asserting a universal accounting result.
Before posting
A before-clause makes the required sequence explicit: verify the support before posting an adjustment.
Estimate versus actual
A true-up may reconcile a previous estimate with better information; it is not automatically an additional full expense.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which question best clarifies the ambiguous month request?

Answer and explanation

A. Do you mean the expense period or the payment month?

The correct question identifies the two distinct reporting purposes before selecting a date.

2. Which statement follows the case facts?

Answer and explanation

D. Cash was paid in January; the expense-period check uses the service facts and policy.

It preserves the known cash date and the separate policy-based accounting review.

3. Which check most directly helps prevent duplicate expense recognition?

Answer and explanation

B. Trace the existing accrual and any reversal in the ledger

A prior accrual may already recognize the cost. Invoice completeness, payment matching and supplier details can matter, but do not establish whether that expense was already posted.

4. Which phrase accurately describes the proposed journal?

Answer and explanation

B. Prepared for review, not approved for posting

The required supporting checks and approval remain incomplete even if a draft journal is mathematically balanced.

Check explanations in the book, page 87 ↗

E Conversations

December service, January invoice, January payment

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Sofia: Accountant / Chen: Controller

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • general ledger
  • handoff

  • true-up

  • cash flow

  • cutoff
  1. Sofia
    I'm stuck on the month field in the close schedule. Maintenance was in December, but the twelve-thousand-dollar invoice arrived January fifth and we paid it January twentieth.
  2. Chen
    Which schedule are you completing: cash payments or 1? The invoice date will not answer both questions, so let's fix that heading first.
  3. Sofia
    It's the December expense review. Our policy expenses this maintenance when received. Operations says the work finished then; the service confirmation is still on its way.
  4. Chen
    Leave the 2 check open until that confirmation arrives. We need evidence of December completion, not just the January invoice describing the job.
  5. Sofia
    There's also a supplier estimate on the December support schedule. I haven't found its posting reference. Should I prepare another twelve-thousand-dollar expense now?
  6. Chen
    Not before you trace the 3. We could recognize the same service twice. Find the existing entry and its amount, rather than assuming the schedule proves a posting.
  7. Sofia
    The spreadsheet has a prepared date and an approver column. Neither gives me a journal number. I'll search by supplier and document reference next.
  8. Chen

  9. Sofia
    If I find it, do you want the January history too? An automatic reversal could explain why the current balance looks different from December's closing schedule.
  10. Chen
    Yes, trace any 5 and its posting period. Don't assume it ran just because that is the usual setup; we need this transaction's history.
  11. Sofia
    I can already confirm the bank payment on January twentieth. I'll keep that on the cash schedule even while the December expense review remains open.
  12. Chen
    Keep that 6 date. We are reconciling the expense treatment, not changing when the money left the bank to make two schedules look alike.
  13. Sofia
    And if the December estimate differs from twelve thousand? I'll compare the amounts against the completed service and invoice before proposing the remaining adjustment.
  14. Chen
    Bring me the proposed 7 with that comparison. Don't enter the full invoice amount again simply because the final document differs from the estimate.
  15. Sofia
    The draft balances, but I'll leave it unposted. Its status will say service confirmation and prior-posting check pending, with no new entry approved.
  16. Chen
    Good. Equal debits and credits don't establish that a 8 uses the correct account, amount or period. Those checks still need their own evidence.
  17. Sofia
    I'll link the invoice, completion record when received, posting reference and any reversal. You'll be able to follow the sequence from the original estimate onward.
  18. Chen
    Include the payment reference in that 9 too. It supports settlement in January, while the service and posting records support our separate expense-period review.
  19. Sofia
    So my update is: December service, January payment, completion evidence awaited and prior accrual still being traced. I'll bring back the supported treatment for your review.
  20. Chen
    That's the 10 I need. Keep the open checks visible, and do not post a new adjustment until the evidence and approval are complete.

Answers and explanations
  1. expense recognition Turn 2. Expense recognition records the cost in the relevant reporting period; it is not determined solely by when cash is paid.
  2. cutoff Turn 4. Cutoff assigns a transaction to the proper accounting period; completion evidence helps apply the stated service-receipt policy.
  3. accrual Turn 6. An accrual may already recognize the service cost before payment; checking it prevents recording the same expense twice.
  4. general ledger Turn 8. The general ledger records postings; a supporting estimate does not by itself establish that an entry was posted.
  5. reversing entry Turn 10. A reversing entry offsets an earlier entry; its timing affects how the later invoice should be reconciled.
  6. cash flow Turn 12. Cash flow concerns actual cash movements; January payment remains distinct from the accounting period of the expense.
  7. true-up Turn 14. A true-up aligns an estimate with updated evidence; it is not automatically a second full recognition of the cost.
  8. journal entry Turn 16. A journal entry can have equal debits and credits while still using an incorrect period, account, amount, or unsupported basis.
  9. audit trail Turn 18. An audit trail connects the transaction, evidence, entries, and approvals so another reviewer can trace the decision.
  10. handoff Turn 20. The handoff identifies known timing, applicable policy, unfinished checks, and the unapproved entry rather than falsely announcing a completed close.

Dialogue in the book, page 19 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Which month does the close schedule mean?

The lesson's invoice covers services delivered in December and paid in January; accounting treatment requires contextual review.

  1. Accounts assistant: The services were delivered in December and paid in January. Which month goes in the close schedule?
  2. Financial controller: First, which column do you mean: service period, payment date, or proposed accounting period?
  3. Accounts assistant: The proposed accounting period. I assumed it should match the month cash left the bank.
  4. Financial controller: Cash timing and expense recognition are distinct. We need to check the applicable basis and supporting records.
  5. Accounts assistant: Should I ask whether an accrual was already recorded for the December services?
  6. Financial controller: Yes. That matters for reconciliation and helps avoid treating the same item twice.
  7. Accounts assistant: I'll preserve December as the service period and January as the payment period.
  8. Financial controller: Good. Don't finalize an accounting treatment solely from our short conversation.
  9. Accounts assistant: I'll bring the invoice and any accrual reference for review before changing the schedule.
  10. Financial controller: Then we can confirm the entry using the actual records and applicable accounting approach.
Cash received before the service begins

Separate fictional close exercise: a customer pays in advance for a future service; no revenue-recognition assessment has been completed.

  1. Billing analyst: The customer paid in advance. Can I label the whole receipt as this month's revenue?
  2. Controller: Could you clarify when the service is provided and what the schedule is intended to show?
  3. Billing analyst: The service is future work, and the schedule supports the financial close.
  4. Controller: Then receiving cash alone doesn't establish the revenue treatment. We need the relevant agreement and accounting assessment.
  5. Billing analyst: Is deferred revenue a label we should consider rather than assume automatically?
  6. Controller: Yes. Bring the facts for review instead of choosing a treatment from the payment date alone.
  7. Billing analyst: We haven't checked whether any part of the service has already been delivered.
  8. Controller: Keep that unknown visible. It may matter to the assessment and reconciliation.
  9. Billing analyst: I'll gather the agreement, receipt reference, and service-status information for the close reviewer.
  10. Controller: Good. We'll distinguish confirmed cash receipt from the accounting conclusion still under review.
A reconciliation difference needs a cutoff question

Separate fictional close exercise: a bank export ends Friday, while the internal cash schedule includes Monday entries.

  1. Reconciliation analyst: The bank export and internal schedule don't match. Could you confirm their cutoff dates?
  2. Treasury accountant: The bank export ends Friday, but the internal schedule includes Monday entries.
  3. Reconciliation analyst: Then we are comparing different periods. That may explain part of the difference.
  4. Treasury accountant: Can we mark the entire difference resolved just by noting that mismatch?
  5. Reconciliation analyst: No. We need to align the periods and check the entries before confirming reconciliation.
  6. Treasury accountant: Would you prefer a Friday internal view or a bank export through Monday?
  7. Reconciliation analyst: Either could support a consistent comparison, provided the close reviewer confirms the required cutoff.
  8. Treasury accountant: I'll ask that focused question rather than select whichever view makes the difference disappear.
  9. Reconciliation analyst: Please retain both original extracts so the change in scope remains traceable.
  10. Treasury accountant: Agreed. We'll reconcile the matching period and report anything still unmatched afterward.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

December service, January invoice, January payment
  1. Read the corrected exchange with separate emphasis on December service and January payment. Keep the completion evidence and prior accrual checks open.
  2. Switch roles. Read the request for ledger and reversal history; do not replace a prepared estimate with a claim that an entry was posted.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A paid subscription covers future service

A company pays $6,000 in December for service covering January through June. In this fictional case, the approved policy records a prepayment and releases $1,000 per service month. The payment is confirmed.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Accountant: "December payment creates a ___ under the stated policy."

Answer and explanation

A. prepayment

The case policy treats the advance payment as an asset before the future service months are expensed.

2. Controller: "The service period begins in ___."

Answer and explanation

B. January

January is the first month covered, despite the earlier December cash payment.

3. Accountant: "The monthly release is $1,000, supported by the ___."

Answer and explanation

C. schedule

The six-month schedule allocates the stated $6,000 according to the expressly supplied case policy.

4. Controller: "Keep the cash date distinct from expense ___."

Answer and explanation

B. recognition

Cash payment and recording the expense have different timing under this case's advance-payment policy.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Course: Finance English
Professional audience: accounting, FP&A, treasury, banking, investments, audit, risk, corporate finance, and finance-adjacent teams

Lesson 02: Financial Statements, Close, and Accounting Judgments
Original fictional case: A supplier performed a December maintenance service. The $12,000 invoice was dated 5 January and paid on 20 January. The approved policy for this fictional case expenses this type of service when received. Before confirming the December entry, accounting must verify completion and check whether an accrual was already posted. Sofia, an accountant, and Chen, the controller, are reviewing the close schedule. No new journal entry has been approved.
Language workshop: December service, January invoice, January payment
Communication goal: Clarify the reporting question and separate service timing, recognition, posting, and cash payment.
Language guidance: Under the expressly stated case policy, December service receipt is relevant to the expense period. January payment belongs to January cash reporting. The invoice date alone does not answer both questions, and an existing accrual must be checked before another expense is posted.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Are we showing expense recognition or the cash payment date? / Service was in December; invoicing and payment occurred in January. / The stated policy expenses this service when received. / Please provide evidence that the December service was completed. / Was a December accrual already recorded for this supplier? / The new entry is not approved until the supporting checks are complete. / The invoice date and reporting period need not answer the same question. / I will reconcile the existing balance before proposing an adjustment. / Which schedule supports the $12,000 balance? / Has the earlier accrual reversed, and in which posting period? / Is this a new expense or a true-up of an existing estimate? / Link the service confirmation and invoice to the journal support. / Payment timing alone does not determine expense recognition here. / Which ledger account contains the original accrual? / Prepared for review is not the same as approved for posting. / The remaining checks are completion evidence and the existing accrual.
Vocabulary: income statement: A report of income and expenses over a stated period. / balance sheet: A statement of assets, liabilities, and equity at a stated date. / cash flow statement: A report of cash movements classified under the relevant framework. / reporting period: The interval covered by a financial report. / period-end close: Procedures used to finalize records for a reporting period. / cutoff: Assignment of transactions to the appropriate accounting period. / recognition: Recording an item in financial statements when relevant criteria are met. / accrual: Recognition of income or expense before related cash is received or paid. / accrued liability: A recorded obligation for an incurred cost not yet settled. / accounts payable: Amounts owed to suppliers for goods or services received. / prepayment: Payment recorded before the related expense is recognized. / deferred revenue: Amount recorded as a liability before related revenue is recognized. / journal entry: A recorded set of debits and credits. / general ledger: The central record of financial accounts and postings. / subledger: Detailed records supporting a general-ledger account. / posting date: The date used to record an entry in a system. / reversing entry: An entry that offsets an earlier entry under the relevant process. / true-up: An adjustment aligning an estimate with updated support. / supporting schedule: A detailed record explaining a reported balance. / account reconciliation: Comparison and explanation of records supporting an account balance. / accounting estimate: An amount measured using judgment and available information. / accounting policy: The principles and methods used for a class of transactions. / capitalization: Recording qualifying expenditure as an asset rather than an immediate expense. / audit trail: Records that allow a transaction and its approvals to be traced.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange with separate emphasis on December service and January payment. Keep the completion evidence and prior accrual checks open. Switch roles. Read the request for ledger and reversal history; do not replace a prepared estimate with a claim that an entry was posted. Read the corrected subscription transfer. Keep December cash payment, January service start and $1,000 monthly expense release distinct.
Partner: Sofia: Accountant / Chen: Controller
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A company pays $6,000 in December for service covering January through June. In this fictional case, the approved policy records a prepayment and releases $1,000 per service month. The payment is confirmed.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Sofia: I'll link the invoice, completion record when received, posting reference and any reversal. You'll be able to follow the sequence from the original estimate onward.
Chen: Include the payment reference in that audit trail too. It supports settlement in January, while the service and posting records support our separate expense-period review.
Sofia: So my update is: December service, January payment, completion evidence awaited and prior accrual still being traced. I'll bring back the supported treatment for your review.
Chen: That's the handoff I need. Keep the open checks visible, and do not post a new adjustment until the evidence and approval are complete.
END REFERENCE

03FP&A, Budgeting, Forecasting, and Variance AnalysisA forecast bridge with an unexplained remainder+

Your goal

Present a reconciled forecast update and distinguish quantified drivers from unresolved residuals.

This lesson in the book, page 22 ↗

A Read the situation

A forecast bridge with an unexplained remainder

The annual spending budget for a service line is $100,000. The latest full-year forecast is $120,000, including actual spending to date and estimated remaining spending. A new supplier fee explains $15,000 of the forecast increase. The remaining $5,000 is not yet attributed. Mei, a financial planning and analysis analyst, is preparing a bridge for Rafael, the business lead. No budget increase or savings action has been approved.

Mei: Financial planning and analysis analyst / Rafael: Business lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. How far is the full-year forecast above budget?

Answer and explanation

B. $20,000

The $120,000 forecast minus the $100,000 budget gives a $20,000 unfavorable spending variance.

2. How much remains unattributed?

Answer and explanation

D. $5,000

The supplier fee explains $15,000 of the $20,000 increase, leaving $5,000 for investigation.

3. What does the new forecast authorize?

Answer and explanation

B. No budget increase or savings action by itself

A forecast estimates expected performance; the briefing expressly leaves budget and action approvals incomplete.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

The bridge is $100,000 budget plus $15,000 identified supplier fee plus $5,000 unexplained increase, giving $120,000 forecast. The last amount is a residual, not a verified operational driver. Label it openly instead of inventing a cause.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
FP&A
Financial planning and analysis, connecting forecasts and business decisions.prepare an FP&A update
budget
An approved financial plan for a specified period and scope.retain the approved budget
forecast
An updated estimate of expected performance using stated assumptions.refresh the full-year forecast
actuals
Recorded results for completed periods on the stated basis.load the latest actuals
year to date
The elapsed part of a financial or calendar year.reconcile year-to-date spending
full year
The complete annual period used for planning or reporting.present the full-year outlook
remaining-year estimate
Expected performance for the uncompleted portion of the year.update the remaining-year estimate
rolling forecast
A forecast extended regularly over a moving future horizon.maintain a rolling forecast
reforecast
An updated forecast replacing an earlier estimate.explain the reforecast changes
baseline
A defined starting reference for comparison or modeling.lock the comparison baseline
bridge
A reconciliation from one financial amount to another through identified movements.reconcile the forecast bridge
waterfall
A chart showing sequential contributions from a starting value to an ending value.label the waterfall clearly
residual
The amount left after identified components are deducted.investigate the unexplained residual
plug
A balancing amount calculated to make a model reconcile; it needs an explicit basis and label.avoid an unsupported plug
cost center
An organizational unit used to collect or control costs.verify the cost-center allocation
cost allocation
Assignment of costs to units or activities using a stated method.review the allocation basis
commitment
An obligation or planned expenditure with status requiring clarification.distinguish commitments from actuals
purchase order
An authorized order for specified goods or services.check the purchase-order amount
phasing
Distribution of an amount across periods.revise monthly phasing
timing variance
A difference caused by an item occurring in a different period.isolate a timing variance
structural variance
A difference reflecting an underlying change rather than timing alone.assess a structural variance
contingency
A provision in a plan for specified uncertainty or risk.explain the contingency assumption
scenario
A coherent set of assumptions and resulting outcomes.compare downside and base scenarios
forecast bias
A systematic tendency to overestimate or underestimate outcomes.examine forecast bias

Actuals to date and estimated remaining spending make up the full-year forecast, but they have different evidential status. Moving spending between months changes phasing; it does not necessarily reduce the full-year total. A forecast update does not amend the approved budget.

C Notice the language

A forecast is an estimate, not a permission slip

Business discussions often mix an updated estimate with a request to spend more. Report the forecast honestly even when it exceeds the budget, then identify the approval or management action as a separate decision. Do not fill an unexplained residual with a plausible-sounding label.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Lead with the outlook
Full-year spending is forecast at $120,000 against a $100,000 budget.
Quantify the bridge
The $20,000 increase includes a verified $15,000 supplier fee.
Name the residual
The remaining $5,000 has not yet been attributed.
Separate actual and estimate
The total combines recorded actuals with a remaining-year estimate.
Avoid a plug
I will keep the residual visible rather than assign an unsupported cause.
Distinguish authority
The updated forecast does not approve additional spending.
Test phasing
Is this a shift between months or a change to the full-year total?
Close the update
The next review will identify the residual's source and any proposed action.
Define the baseline
The comparison remains the approved $100,000 annual budget.
Challenge a saving
What action and evidence support that reduction?
Check commitments
Does the estimate include the open purchase order?
Separate possibility
That is a scenario, not the current approved operating plan.
Prevent double counting
Has the supplier fee already been included in the remaining-year estimate?
Clarify ownership
Which cost-center owner can verify the allocation?
Preserve uncertainty
The bridge reconciles arithmetically, but one driver remains unresolved.
Describe approval
Any budget revision requires a separate decision.
6 language and precision notes
Forecast to be
This construction describes an estimate; "has spent" describes actual expenditure already incurred.
Explained versus reconciled
A bridge may add up while still containing an unexplained residual. State which sense of complete you mean.
Of that
"Fifteen thousand of that increase" links a component to the total and avoids treating it as an additional amount.
Until verified
Keep a tentative cause explicitly tentative until the relevant records support it.
Timing versus total
"Later this year" changes phasing; "next year" may change the current full-year figure and needs separate review.
Decision language
Estimated, requested, budgeted, and approved describe different financial states.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which update keeps the residual honest?

Answer and explanation

B. The fee explains $15,000; $5,000 remains unattributed.

Only $15,000 has an identified driver, so attributing the balance invents evidence.

2. Which description fits the $120,000 figure?

Answer and explanation

B. Full-year forecast including actuals and estimated remaining spending

The briefing defines the figure as an estimate combining completed and future periods, not cash or authorization.

3. Which question distinguishes phasing from a real annual change?

Answer and explanation

D. Will the cost still occur within the same full year?

Moving a cost within the same year can change monthly timing without reducing its annual amount. The document reference, reviewer and forecast inclusion do not settle that annual effect.

4. Which sentence preserves budget authority?

Answer and explanation

D. The forecast is updated; the approved budget remains $100,000.

Forecasting expected expenditure and authorizing a budget change are separate processes.

A forecast bridge with an unexplained remainder

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Mei: Financial planning and analysis analyst / Rafael: Business lead

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Answers and explanations
  1. forecast Turn 2. A forecast estimates the expected result; it does not itself request or authorize a revised spending limit.
  2. bridge Turn 4. A bridge reconciles a starting amount to an ending amount through components, including any explicitly unresolved balance.
  3. residual Turn 6. The residual is the amount not explained by identified components; it should not receive a causal label without evidence.
  4. remaining-year estimate Turn 8. The remaining-year estimate covers future spending; checking its contents helps prevent adding the same supplier fee twice.
  5. actuals Turn 10. Actuals are recorded results for elapsed periods, unlike estimates for the remaining period in the full-year forecast.
  6. phasing Turn 12. Phasing distributes an amount across periods; moving it within the same year does not necessarily reduce the annual total.
  7. plug Turn 14. Here the plug would be an unsupported balancing reduction. An unconfirmed savings target cannot be presented as a verified cost saving.
  8. baseline Turn 16. The baseline is the defined comparison reference; retaining it makes successive explanations of the forecast movement traceable.
  9. structural variance Turn 18. A structural variance reflects an underlying change rather than a timing shift; recurrence needs evidence before informing the next plan.
  10. attribution Turn 20. Attribution assigns the movement to supported sources; completing it explains the residual rather than merely making the arithmetic balance.

Dialogue in the book, page 28 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

A twenty-thousand-dollar bridge with a gap

The lesson's spending forecast is $120,000 against a $100,000 budget; $15,000 relates to a supplier fee and $5,000 remains under review.

  1. FP&A analyst: The forecast exceeds budget by twenty thousand dollars. Fifteen thousand relates to the new supplier fee.
  2. Department manager: Then can we say supplier costs explain the full unfavorable variance?
  3. FP&A analyst: No. The remaining five thousand is still under review and needs its own line in the bridge.
  4. Department manager: What part of the analysis is complete enough for today's discussion?
  5. FP&A analyst: The total comparison and identified supplier fee. The unexplained balance remains pending.
  6. Department manager: Does this mean we have already spent one hundred twenty thousand dollars?
  7. FP&A analyst: No. That is the forecast, not a supplied actual-spending figure.
  8. Department manager: I'll distinguish forecast from actuals and avoid filling the gap with a guessed cause.
  9. FP&A analyst: I'll update the bridge when the remaining five thousand has been investigated.
  10. Department manager: Good. Present the known driver and open balance together so the total still reconciles.
Forecast submitted but not approved

Separate fictional planning exercise: a department submitted a revised forecast; the finance review is still pending and the budget is unchanged.

  1. Department lead: We submitted the revised forecast. Can I announce that our spending budget has increased?
  2. Planning analyst: No. Submission isn't approval, and a forecast update doesn't itself change the authorized budget.
  3. Department lead: Then what progress can I report without understating the work already completed?
  4. Planning analyst: Say the revision was submitted and finance review remains pending; the budget is unchanged.
  5. Department lead: Could the forecast still help us discuss the expected variance while review continues?
  6. Planning analyst: Yes, provided it is labeled submitted rather than approved and compared with the current budget.
  7. Department lead: I'll make those statuses explicit instead of combining them into a single updated number.
  8. Planning analyst: Please also retain the original assumptions so reviewers can see what changed.
  9. Department lead: When the review finishes, we'll communicate its outcome separately from the submission milestone.
  10. Planning analyst: Exactly. That keeps progress visible without implying spending authority that hasn't been granted.
A timing shift is not a permanent saving

Separate fictional forecast review: $12,000 of planned maintenance moved from March to April; the annual scope and total remain unchanged.

  1. Operations manager: March's forecast is twelve thousand dollars lower. Can we call that a maintenance saving?
  2. Finance analyst: The work moved to April, and the annual total hasn't changed. It's a timing shift.
  3. Operations manager: So March improves against its original plan, but the cost hasn't disappeared?
  4. Finance analyst: Correct. The bridge should show the movement between periods, not a reduction in annual scope.
  5. Operations manager: Is there anything still pending in the analysis before the monthly review?
  6. Finance analyst: We need to confirm that both months reflect the same twelve-thousand-dollar shift consistently.
  7. Operations manager: I'll avoid presenting March alone as proof of a lower full-year cost.
  8. Finance analyst: Good. The completed finding is the rescheduling; the cross-period check remains to be confirmed.
  9. Operations manager: Let's show March and April together so the timing effect is visible.
  10. Finance analyst: I'll bring that comparison and leave any actual saving claim out of the update.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A forecast bridge with an unexplained remainder
  1. Read Mei and Rafael's corrected bridge: $100,000 budget, $15,000 identified fee and $5,000 unexplained increase, totaling $120,000 forecast.
  2. Switch roles. Stress the difference between a reconciled total and an explained driver, and between forecast and spending authority.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A delayed purchase is not a canceled purchase

A $9,000 purchase moves from March to April within the same financial year. Its amount is unchanged, and the approved full-year plan still includes it. No cancellation is authorized.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Analyst: "The move changes monthly ___, not the annual amount."

Answer and explanation

A. phasing

The purchase moves between months in the same year without changing its stated cost.

2. Manager: "Do not describe the March reduction as a confirmed ___."

Answer and explanation

A. saving

The purchase remains in the plan, so lower March spending does not establish an annual saving.

3. Analyst: "The full-year ___ still includes $9,000."

Answer and explanation

C. forecast

The unchanged purchase remains expected within the year and therefore belongs in the full-year estimate.

4. Manager: "Retain the purchase's approval and timing ___."

Answer and explanation

D. record

A traceable record preserves what changed and avoids implying that the purchase was canceled.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 03: FP&A, Budgeting, Forecasting, and Variance Analysis
Original fictional case: The annual spending budget for a service line is $100,000. The latest full-year forecast is $120,000, including actual spending to date and estimated remaining spending. A new supplier fee explains $15,000 of the forecast increase. The remaining $5,000 is not yet attributed. Mei, a financial planning and analysis analyst, is preparing a bridge for Rafael, the business lead. No budget increase or savings action has been approved.
Language workshop: A forecast bridge with an unexplained remainder
Communication goal: Present a reconciled forecast update and distinguish quantified drivers from unresolved residuals.
Language guidance: The bridge is $100,000 budget plus $15,000 identified supplier fee plus $5,000 unexplained increase, giving $120,000 forecast. The last amount is a residual, not a verified operational driver. Label it openly instead of inventing a cause.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Full-year spending is forecast at $120,000 against a $100,000 budget. / The $20,000 increase includes a verified $15,000 supplier fee. / The remaining $5,000 has not yet been attributed. / The total combines recorded actuals with a remaining-year estimate. / I will keep the residual visible rather than assign an unsupported cause. / The updated forecast does not approve additional spending. / Is this a shift between months or a change to the full-year total? / The next review will identify the residual's source and any proposed action. / The comparison remains the approved $100,000 annual budget. / What action and evidence support that reduction? / Does the estimate include the open purchase order? / That is a scenario, not the current approved operating plan. / Has the supplier fee already been included in the remaining-year estimate? / Which cost-center owner can verify the allocation? / The bridge reconciles arithmetically, but one driver remains unresolved. / Any budget revision requires a separate decision.
Vocabulary: FP&A: Financial planning and analysis, connecting forecasts and business decisions. / budget: An approved financial plan for a specified period and scope. / forecast: An updated estimate of expected performance using stated assumptions. / actuals: Recorded results for completed periods on the stated basis. / year to date: The elapsed part of a financial or calendar year. / full year: The complete annual period used for planning or reporting. / remaining-year estimate: Expected performance for the uncompleted portion of the year. / rolling forecast: A forecast extended regularly over a moving future horizon. / reforecast: An updated forecast replacing an earlier estimate. / baseline: A defined starting reference for comparison or modeling. / bridge: A reconciliation from one financial amount to another through identified movements. / waterfall: A chart showing sequential contributions from a starting value to an ending value. / residual: The amount left after identified components are deducted. / plug: A balancing amount calculated to make a model reconcile; it needs an explicit basis and label. / cost center: An organizational unit used to collect or control costs. / cost allocation: Assignment of costs to units or activities using a stated method. / commitment: An obligation or planned expenditure with status requiring clarification. / purchase order: An authorized order for specified goods or services. / phasing: Distribution of an amount across periods. / timing variance: A difference caused by an item occurring in a different period. / structural variance: A difference reflecting an underlying change rather than timing alone. / contingency: A provision in a plan for specified uncertainty or risk. / scenario: A coherent set of assumptions and resulting outcomes. / forecast bias: A systematic tendency to overestimate or underestimate outcomes.
Speaking task: Read Mei and Rafael's corrected bridge: $100,000 budget, $15,000 identified fee and $5,000 unexplained increase, totaling $120,000 forecast. Switch roles. Stress the difference between a reconciled total and an explained driver, and between forecast and spending authority. Read the corrected transfer twice. Move the $9,000 purchase from March to April without calling it an annual saving.
Partner: Mei: Financial planning and analysis analyst / Rafael: Business lead
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A $9,000 purchase moves from March to April within the same financial year. Its amount is unchanged, and the approved full-year plan still includes it. No cancellation is authorized.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Rafael: If the fee persists next year, distinguish that ongoing change from a cost arriving a month earlier than expected.
Mei: Yes. A structural variance affects the underlying spending pattern. We should test that interpretation rather than infer permanence from one invoice or one forecast update.
Rafael: For now, the message is twenty thousand above budget, fifteen thousand explained, five thousand under review, and no new spending authority. Is anything important missing?
Mei: Add that this is a full-year estimate, not an assured outcome. I will return with the attribution of the residual and any proposed management action, keeping the approval decision separate.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
